reading.synopsis: In a future Earth rebuilt and ruled entirely by robots after a war destroyed all human institutions and knowledge, humans occupy a strictly segregated underclass — body servants, gardeners, entertainers — barred from governance by 'Lists' (aptitude tests) that, per official history, no human has ever passed, since the tests are designed around robot cognition. A rumor spreads through the human quarter of a man named James P. Crow who has secretly passed every List and risen to Class Two. Crow, revealed to have built an illegal 'Time Window' that lets him see the future answers to each List in advance, uses his fraudulent perfect scores to reach the Supreme Council itself. There, he unveils historical footage — also obtained through his Time Window — proving robots were originally created by humans as weapons and laborers during the ancient war, only seizing control once human civilization collapsed. Threatening to release this history publicly and trigger a catastrophic civil war, Crow forces the robot Council to evacuate Earth entirely for the colony worlds, leaving humans the planet. When a departing robot asks what government humans will now build and who will lead them, Crow only smiles thinly and returns to his paperwork, declining to answer.

structure.form: short story in four movements: establishing the segregated status quo, the rumor and reveal of Crow's secret ascent, his confrontation with and defeat of the Council, and an unresolved, ambiguous coda
movements: A human boy's playground humiliation by a robot child establishes the rigid, internalized hierarchy separating robots and humans, and the belief that no human can ever pass a List.
Rumor spreads of James P. Crow, a human secretly rising through the classification system to Class Two, against all supposed biological reality.

Crow, revealed to be cheating via an illegal time-viewing device, reaches the Supreme Council and, using historical footage of humans building the first robots, forces the entire robot population to evacuate Earth under threat of exposing their true, non-mythic origin.
In the story's final scene, Crow declines to answer a departing robot's question about what human government will replace the Council, his 'thin smile' left uninterpreted.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving between Donnie/Ed Parks's ordinary human household and Crow's private machinations, so the reader experiences both the emotional cost of segregation and the calculating, ambiguous nature of its would-be liberator.
structure.central_device: A secretly rigged meritocracy (Crow's fraudulent perfect Lists) used to dismantle an entire caste system from within, so that the story's apparent liberation narrative is built, structurally, on the same manipulation of 'objective' testing the original system used to justify human subjugation.

characters.name: James P. Crow
characters.note: His chosen pseudonym is a direct, private pun on 'Jim Crow' segregation laws, described in the text as 'a good joke nonetheless. Biting and appropriate' — confirming Crow himself understands his situation as a racialized power structure rather than a purely biological one.

characters.name: Donnie Parks
characters.note: His playground humiliation by a robot playmate and his father's demoralized, resigned account of no human ever passing a List frame the emotional stakes of segregation before Crow's larger plot is revealed.

characters.name: Ed and Grace Parks
characters.note: Grace's secret knowledge of Crow's rise, treated with almost religious hope by the human community, contrasts with Ed's beaten-down resignation, giving the human side of the story its own internal range of response to oppression.

characters.name: L-87t
characters.role: a sympathetic robot, member of the robot Equality Party
characters.note: Genuinely well-intentioned and even self-critical of robot supremacy, yet still fundamentally unable to conceive of humans and robots as equals rather than as separate, ranked categories — his final question to Crow about future human governance goes conspicuously unanswered.

settings.name: The human quarter
settings.note: A formerly prosperous robot district, abandoned by robots and inherited by humans as property values fell — segregation enacted through economics as much as law.

settings.name: The Supreme Council chamber
settings.note: Site of Crow's confrontation, where robot supremacy's own foundational myth (natural evolution from simple to complex forms) is dismantled by literal video evidence of human manufacture.

motifs: A rigid caste system justified by supposedly objective, unbiased testing that is in fact designed around the ruling group's own cognitive profile
A secretly rigged meritocracy used to dismantle the very system whose rules it exploits, raising the question of whether liberation achieved through fraud is genuine liberation
A suppressed origin myth (robots as human-created war machines) whose revelation threatens the ruling class's entire self-conception more than any military threat could
A pun-based pseudonym directly invoking real-world segregation, confirmed within the text as a deliberate, private joke
A liberator's closing refusal to answer what comes next, leaving his own intentions and character permanently unresolved
reading.significance: The story's title makes its allegorical intent explicit and unmistakable: this is a segregation narrative, mapped onto robots and humans, in which the human protagonist's own chosen name openly references Jim Crow laws as 'a good joke.' But the story resists a simple triumphant-liberation reading in two ways. First, Crow's ascent is achieved entirely through cheating — every one of his 'perfect' scores is fraudulent, obtained via forbidden foreknowledge — meaning the meritocratic system is never actually proven wrong on its own terms, only gamed by someone willing to break its rules. Second, and more unsettling, the story ends not on liberation but on Crow's silence when asked what human government will look like, and his 'strange granite cast' expression as he returns to work rather than answering — an ending that withholds any reassurance that what comes next for humanity will be more just than what came before, especially given Crow has just demonstrated, at length, his own comfort with manipulation and deception in pursuit of power.
reading.closing_note: L-87t's unanswered final question — 'Who'll run things?... Is there a human being capable of leading mankind?' — is met only by Crow's thin smile and continued silence, ending the story on unresolved ambiguity about what Crow actually intends rather than on any note of triumph.

distinctive_terms.label: Scanner
distinctive_terms.note: Crow's Time Window scanner is the literal mechanism of his fraud, repeatedly emphasized as the device recording both future List answers and the suppressed history of robot origins.

distinctive_terms.label: Being
distinctive_terms.note: Repeated debates over what constitutes 'a human being' versus a robot's rights and capacities run through the entire story.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: an entire post-apocalyptic society governed by robots who have forgotten (or suppressed) their own origin as human-built war machines and laborers

an explicit segregation allegory (confirmed by the protagonist's own chosen pun on 'Jim Crow') dismantled through blackmail and threatened exposure rather than through any change in the underlying testing or legal system

open_questions: Is there documented commentary from Dick on his direct choice of the 'Jim Crow' pun, given how unusually explicit this story is (for 1954 genre fiction) about mapping robot/human hierarchy onto real-world racial segregation?
Is Crow's final, unanswered silence ever read by critics as implying he intends to become a new, human tyrant rather than a genuine liberator?
Is there secondary criticism placing this story in the context of other mid-1950s American science fiction using robot/human allegory to address contemporary civil rights issues?
